title: Sterile enclave update window and hw capacity scan - Novara Therapeutics
summary: Initial intake for an air-gapped / sterile-enclave private deployment. Discussed hardware baseline, signed-image update process, chain-of-custody for offline updates, telemetry constraints, and a rough timeline for a pilot. Customer is leaning private on-prem with strict no-egress policy; exploring minimal control-plane connectivity or fully offline private control plane. Action items include sending security pack, proposed signed-update workflow diagram, and capacity estimate spreadsheet.
topics: signed bundles and HSM key injection
transcript:
[00:00] Jared Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we wanted to kick off with quick intros. I'm Jared, AE at Redwood. Priya and Omar from our infra team are here.
[00:14] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Hi, Lena here. I'll be our PM on the project. Marcus here with security, Aisha is our ML lead.
[00:23] Marcus Bell: Marcus, CISO. Uh, quick note: we expect strict no outbound connections from the inference nodes.
[00:30] Priya Shah: Right, understood. Redwood's private offering supports customer-managed networking and fully isolated control planes. We do want to understand the exact update constraints you have.
[00:45] Noor Patel: For updates, the requirement is: images and patches delivered on physical media with SHA-256 signatures. Chain-of-custody is important; we need proof of delivery and tamper evidence.
[00:58] Omar Ruiz: Okay, that's doable. We typically package signed delta bundles that can be applied offline. We support signed full images and incremental patch bundles. How often are you expecting patch windows?
[01:12] Samir Rao: Ideally quarterly for security patches, but model updates maybe monthly — those can be handled during our maintenance windows. We also need the ability to roll back quickly if a model causes performance regressions.
[01:26] Priya Shah: Got it. For rollbacks we keep KV cache compatibility and version pinning so you can pin a model artifact and revert to a prior stable image. Quick question: will the island be on-prem with HSMs for key injection?
[01:40] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Yes, we have an on-prem HSM cluster and a corporate KMS. We cannot rely on cloud KMS. Keys must be injected locally and never leave the airgapped net.
[01:54] Jared Kim: So the flow we recommend: Redwood produces a signed artifact, we hand it to your ops team, you use your HSM to sign or wrap keys, and you deploy. We can provide tooling to validate signatures before staging.
[02:09] Marcus Bell: Validate tooling is important. Also, what's the telemetry footprint? We can accept only aggregated metrics — no raw prompts, no logs containing customer PII, and preferably no model token traces.
[02:23] Omar Ruiz: Understood. For private deployments we can run with telemetry completely disabled, or with a narrow aggregated metrics endpoint that runs in your control plane. If you prefer zero egress, all telemetry can be stored locally and exported manually.
[02:40] Aisha Khan: On the hardware front: we're trying to decide between a smaller H100 pool vs a larger A100-ish fleet; cost and inference latency tradeoffs. Our peak batch size patterns are small, lots of single request low-latency traffic.
[02:55] Priya Shah: For low-latency single-token roundtrips, H100 has advantages especially for longer context; but if you primarily run trimmed quantized models 8-bit, A100-sized nodes can be more cost-effective. Also depends on model choice — some open models we've seen run better on A100 with optimized kernels.
[03:13] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Do you support multi-instance GPUs or MIG-like partitions? We need to consolidate smaller workloads while maintaining isolation across teams.
[03:24] Omar Ruiz: We support partitioning strategies and VM-based isolation; on NVIDIA we can use MIG and also software-based microvms. The runtime supports affinity policies so requests for particular tenants can be pinned.
[03:36] Samir Rao: About the initial seed: can we do a sneakernet load? i.e., ship a pre-loaded cache and models on encrypted SSDs and plug into the nodes to accelerate first-run?
[03:46] Priya Shah: Yes, we often do that for air-gapped customers — a pre-seeded KV cache and model artifacts on encrypted drives. We recommend verifying checksums and signatures on arrival.
[03:57] Marcus Bell: What about firmware and BIOS updates? Those are in our scope too — they need to be validated by our OEM process.
[04:06] Omar Ruiz: We don't manage firmware updates; that's on your hardware team. We can provide guidance for compatibility and a list of vetted NIC/BIOS revisions.
[04:16] Jared Kim: Back to update windows — do you have a preferred maintenance SLA? Can we assume a 4-hour nightly window for patching, or do you only allow longer scheduled quarterly windows?
[04:28] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Nightly windows are tricky; ops runs a nightly backup. We prefer scheduled weekend windows, 6–8 hours. For emergency critical CVEs we need a 24–48 hour mitigation path.
[04:41] Priya Shah: We can design the rollout to support canaries in isolated racks or even an isolated staging cluster within your enclave. If emergency patches are required, we can also provide a hotfix delta that can be applied in under an hour once transferred.
[04:56] Aisha Khan: About model regressions: we want a replayable evaluation harness. Can Redwood package the exact inference binary and inputs used so we can run the same tests offline?
[05:08] Priya Shah: Absolutely. We track model bundles, exact runtime versions, and seed the evaluation harness. We can provide artifacts and an automated regression test suite that runs locally.
[05:20] Marcus Bell: On auditability — we need detailed immutable logs of who initiated an update, what signature was used, who physically handled the media. Does Redwood integrate with our internal SIEM?
[05:33] Omar Ruiz: We can emit signed audit logs that you can ingest. For air-gapped setups you can pull logs from the node and push into your SIEM. We also support hardware-backed attestation for binaries where the node signs boot status.
[05:46] Dr. Lena Ortiz: How do you handle license telemetry? We can't have contact with Redwood hosted license servers.
[05:52] Jared Kim: For Private we offer an offline license file that you can provision, or a time-limited license bound to HW fingerprints. No periodic outbound check-ins required unless you opt into hosted license management.
[06:06] Samir Rao: Great. One last question on fallback: if a cluster becomes unhealthy, can Redwood route traffic to a standby cluster in another site that is also air-gapped?
[06:17] Priya Shah: Yes, multi-site deployment is supported. You can set up a cold standby that is kept in sync via physical media transfers, or a warm standby with occasional syncs. We can support automatic failover, but the enforcement of cross-site data movement must be approved by you.
[06:33] Marcus Bell: Competitors we looked at had varying support for signed updates. Anthropic's partner X had a partial solution; another vendor wanted persistent outbound tunnels which is a no-go.
[06:45] Jared Kim: Noted. We'll make sure to highlight our fully offline workflows in the security pack.
[06:52] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Can you sketch the suggested architecture? We want details on control plane placement, whether it can be a virtual appliance, and what day-2 ops look like.
[07:03] Priya Shah: We'll send a diagram. Quick verbal: option A — private control plane appliance in your management VLAN that has no internet route, used for job orchestration and signed artifact hosting. Option B — fully delegate control plane to your team and run isolated inference-only nodes; Redwood provides tooling as binaries. Option A gives easier observability, Option B gives maximum air-gap.
[07:24] Aisha Khan: For benchmarking, can Redwood run an offline bench harness against our workloads? We want p95 latency numbers and token/sec throughput for our prompts.
[07:34] Omar Ruiz: Yes — we can provide a bench harness zip that you run locally. If you prefer Redwood to do the runs, we can ship an encrypted runner appliance you connect, and we retrieve results via physical media.
[07:48] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Timeline — we want a pilot by end of Q1 '28. Is that feasible?
[07:55] Jared Kim: Feasible. We need to finalize NDA, security questionnaire, and the capacity spreadsheet. We'll propose a pilot of 3 nodes (or one smaller staging + two production) depending on your model selection.
[08:08] Marcus Bell: Next — legal wants to confirm data residency and indemnities. We'll send a standard entitlements doc.
[08:18] Priya Shah: We normally collect a SOC2 pack, architecture diagram, and our signed-update workflow. We'll include an offline-install checklist.
[08:28] Noor Patel: One detail — we have an internal change board that requires playbooks for rollbacks. Can you produce an automated rollback playbook artifact?
[08:38] Priya Shah: Yes, we can provide a step-by-step rollback playbook that is runbook-style and includes verification checksums and health probes to validate success.
[08:48] Aisha Khan: Also: token accounting — we must be able to chargeback by team. Is multi-tenant metering possible with zero egress?
[08:58] Omar Ruiz: Metering can be local. We provide token logs and per-tenant usage files that you can ingest; no outbound required.
[09:08] Jared Kim: Alright, let's recap. We'll send security pack, signed-update workflow diagram, capacity spreadsheet and bench harness, and a proposal for pilot nodes plus an SOW draft. Any other items?
[09:23] Dr. Lena Ortiz: Please include a sample chain-of-custody form and recommended OEM firmware baseline.
[09:30] Marcus Bell: Also include a note about HSM key injection; how we validate the wrapped keys.
[09:36] Priya Shah: We'll include both options: key-wrapping in your HSM and offline sealed key injection.
[09:44] Jared Kim: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with materials and propose dates for a bench run.
[09:50] Noor Patel: Thanks, bye.
[52:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap; some product names may be transcribed slightly off (e.g., "Redwood dedicate" for Dedicated).
